text:
The drive down to Hartwell took four hours in July, through a county that had given up on its grass. The corn stood brown at the edges of the fields, the creek beds cracked and pale, and the air coming off the asphalt had a weight to it. My mother's house sat on a short street of eleven houses, most occupied by people who had lived there since before the interstate was built. I parked and sat in the car for a while, because the porch was already radiating heat.

She came out when she heard me, not when she saw me. That had been her way for decades: the engine, the gravel, and then the door. She was eighty-one and stood in the doorway with her arms crossed and her hair still set, and she said, "You're late," which was not true, because I had left home three hours early to beat the traffic, but it was what she said, and it meant she was glad.

The kitchen was cool with the screens up and the ceiling fan turning. She made lemonade the way she had always made it, ice in the glasses, not the pitcher, her rule since I was small. She cut lemon rounds into the glasses and told me about the drought, which was not news, but she told it as if it were, because news was what the kitchen was for.

"You'll want to sit on the good chair," she said, the second thing she always said, after the lemonade. It was the one with the faded cover of roses, bought the year after my father died, and she had been saving it for company for thirty years, which is to say she had sat in it herself every day and told guests it was better for their backs. The radio played from the living room, the same hour of music every day and then the weather. She told me the hardware store had a new owner who did not know which screws went in which fences, and that Darlene next door had put a roof on her garage, an extravagance, said in the tone she used for extravagances, which was the tone she used for most things.

"Your brother called," she said. "Sunday. He asked if I had the furnace fixed."

"You know Gerry doesn't visit in July," I said.

"Gerry doesn't visit in any month," she said. "He sends a card for my birthday now. He said the card was hard to find. He said he looked in the attic."

I laughed, and she laughed too, a sound that started in her chest and finished before it reached her face.

After lunch, a sandwich on white bread because the refrigerator held mostly her lemonade and her jam, we walked around the neighborhood. It took her longer than it used to, but she walked, and she pointed things out the way she had when I was small. She was careful on the crosswalks now and held the neighbor's fence when she crossed, but she did not let anyone help her, and I did not mention that the heat was getting to her, and she did not either, because mentioning it was the beginning of arrangements, and arrangements were the thing we both avoided.

In the evening we sat on the porch with the fan and the screens up, and she told me about the tomatoes, going poorly, and the blackberries, going well. She asked about my life in pieces, never the big questions. Did the roof leak anymore. Was the school good. She never asked whether I were happy, and I was grateful, because the honest answer would have been complicated and she had no obligation to carry it.

I slept in the guest room under the quilt that had belonged to her mother, and woke at four in the morning sweating, listening to the house tick and the fan turn, and thought about the jam on the counter, the blackberry, which she had started the week before, and decided I would get it in the morning, on the way out.

I left at nine. She walked me to the car and stood in the shade of the awning and watched me put on my seat belt, a habit of hers, as if I were a child leaving on a school bus. I did not get the jam. There was a reason, or there was no reason, and either way I drove four hours back with the thought of the jar on her counter, telling myself she had plenty, that she made it every year, that it would be there when I came back.

I got the call on a Tuesday. The mail carrier had found her slumped in the shade of the shed, in the rows where she had been pruning, and her temperature was something the nurse described in a way I have never managed to repeat exactly. They called it heatstroke. My mother called it sunstroke, which is what you were supposed to call it when she was young. She said she had been looking at the tomatoes, had sat down, that there was no reason to be worried, and then she said, "Tell Gerry I'm fine," which was the first thing she had said to me that month that sounded like anything at all.

She was in the hospital a week, a rehab center another, and then home with a walker she refused to use on the stairs and a nurse aide twice a week. The month between our calls was a month of my mother reporting everything was fine and of me believing her the way you believe a weather report from a town you love. Gerry called and asked about her insurance. I drove down twice and turned around at the edge of town both times, which I do not say in my defense. I say it because it is what happened.

A month after the first visit I drove down again. Four hours, the same brown county, the same cracked creek beds, the same place on the same street of eleven houses.

She opened the door herself. Slower now, wearing a scarf indoors, which I understood later was a burn on her neck that embarrassed her, but she stood there with her arms crossed and said, "You're late," and I said, "You said that last time," and she said, "I said it then and I say it now," the closest she came to being warm.

The house was changed in ways that took me a while to inventory. The porch furniture was covered with tarps. The screens were up and latched, every one. The garden had gone to seed, the tomatoes drowning in their own vines, the blackberries a tangle she had left alone. The air inside was cool and smelled like lemonade and vanilla, the smell of her kitchen, unchanged except quieter, the radio playing the same hour of music at the same hour of the day.

And then the remnants. My mug was on the counter where I had left it. She had washed it, which was the thing that struck me, because she had washed it and not put it away. She had put it back where it had been, facing the same direction, and left it there a month, a month of mornings in which she must have passed it and not moved it.

My book was on the couch, open. A paperback I had read on the drive down, the kind of novel I buy to be polite to myself. I asked if she had gotten into it, and she said, "I read the first part. Then I couldn't get back into it," and I believed her, because she was honest about her own limits in a way she had never been honest about anything else.

And the photograph on the mantel, the one of my children, which had faced the living room for years, faced the front door now. "I turned it toward the door," she said. "I like it better from here."

And the jam. The blackberry jar sat on the kitchen table, in the light, lid off, its surface dented with the pattern of a spoon, dented many times, in rows, in the orderly fashion of a person rationing something. "I've been eating it slow," she said. "One spoonful a day. That's how it's supposed to be done."

I sat down at the table. She cut two slices of white bread and spread the jam on them with a butter knife, and we ate, and outside the screens the sun was doing what it had been doing all summer, and the fan turned in the living room. She told me about the nurse aide, kind but late, and the walker, which she had finally agreed to use on the stairs, and Gerry, who had called again and asked whether I had fixed anything in the house.

"You should have taken the jar with you," she said, no accusation in it, only the practical arithmetic of her kitchen, where every jar had a purpose. "I'd have made more."

I told her I had thought she had plenty. She looked at me over the rim of her lemonade glass, ice clinking, and said, "You thought that, did you," in the tone she used for extravagances, for the roof on the garage, for the things people believed about her that she could not afford to correct.

I did not argue. I drank my lemonade and ate the second spoonful of jam and watched her watch me eat it, and understood, sitting there at her table in the heat of August, that the visit had not ended when I got in the car. It had been sitting on her counter, in her mug and her book and her photograph and her rationed spoonfuls, for a month, while she kept it alive the only way she knew how, which was by using it, a little at a time, like a good thing.

When I stood up to leave, I did not go to the sink. I had washed her dishes for twenty years, every visit, sweeping the crumbs off the counter and putting the glasses in the drying rack and leaving the kitchen cleaner than I found it, a ritual done so many times I had stopped noticing I was doing it. This time I left the dishes in the sink, both glasses, the butter knife, the bread plate, and walked out to the car and put on my seat belt while she watched from the awning, and she said, "Don't worry about them. I'll do them tonight," which was a lie, because she had trouble with the jam spoon, and we both knew it, and neither of us said anything.

The drive back took three hours and forty minutes. I did not look in the rearview mirror at the end, because there was nothing there to see except a house with the screens up, keeping out the heat, like every other house on the street.
